lead: The conjugate beam method turns deflection into statics. Replace the real beam with a fictitious conjugate beam of the same length. Load it with the M/EI diagram of the real beam. Then the conjugate shear equals the real slope, and the conjugate moment equals the real deflection. It exists because statics is faster than integrating the elastic curve. It is used for quick checks on determinate beams. Only a few universities teach it.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for the elastic curve and 5.4 for M/EI areas.

blocks.text: Take the real beam of length L. Draw its bending moment M(x). Divide every ordinate by EI, where E is Young's modulus and I is the second moment of area. The result is the M/EI diagram, with unit 1/m. Make a conjugate beam of length L and load it with q*(x)=M(x)/EI. The conjugate shear V*(x) and moment M*(x) obey dV*/dx=q* and dM*/dx=V*. Comparing with dθ/dx=M/EI and dy/dx=θ gives V*=θ and M*=y. Here θ is real slope in radians and y is real deflection in metres. Some syllabi call this the fictitious beam method; the standard name is the conjugate beam method. Choose one sign convention: sagging M positive, downward y positive. Apply the M/EI load in the direction that keeps the signs consistent. Check one known value before trusting the rest.

Transform every real support. A real fixed end has θ=0 and y=0, so the conjugate must have V*=0 and M*=0: a free end. A real free end has θ≠0 and y≠0, so the conjugate must have V*≠0 and M*≠0: a fixed end. A real simple support has y=0 but θ≠0, so the conjugate has M*=0 but V*≠0: a simple support. A real internal hinge has y=0 and a possible jump in slope, so the conjugate has M*=0 and a possible jump in shear: an internal hinge. Never keep the real supports. After loading, V* at any section is the real slope, and M* is the real deflection. The method is for determinate beams: a simply supported beam with a central load, or a cantilever with an end load. Indeterminate beams need M found first; see 5.8.

figure.caption: Each real support is swapped for its conjugate support before the M/EI load is applied. Notice that fixed and free ends exchange roles.

spec.aria: A tree lists how each real support is replaced by its conjugate support.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of span 6 m carries a central point load of 12 kN. EI = 5000 kN·m². Use the conjugate beam method to find the support slope and the midspan deflection.
steps: By symmetry, each real reaction is R = P/2 = 12/2 = 6 kN.
For 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 m, M(x)=R x=6x kN·m. At midspan, Mmax=6×3=18 kN·m.
M/EI diagram: peak = 18/5000 = 0.0036 m⁻¹; zero at both ends, two triangles.
Real simple supports become conjugate simple supports. Span = 6 m. Load q*=M/EI.
Total conjugate load = area = ½ × 6 × 0.0036 = 0.0108. Each conjugate reaction V* = 0.0108/2 = 0.0054 rad.
This V* is the real support slope: θ = 0.0054 rad.
Left half load area = 0.0054. Its centroid is 1 m from midspan. Conjugate moment at midspan: M* = 0.0054×3 − 0.0054×1 = 0.0108 m.
Thus midspan deflection y = 0.0108 m = 10.8 mm downward.
examples.answer: Support slope θ = 0.0054 rad; midspan deflection y = 0.0108 m = 10.8 mm downward.
examples.check:
P=12.0
L=6.0
EI=5000.0
Mmax=P*L/4
curv=Mmax/EI
area=0.5*L*curv
Rstar=area/2
theta=Rstar
Mstar=Rstar*(L/2)-(area/2)*(L/6)
def_m=Mstar
def_mm=def_m*1000
print(round(theta,4))
print(round(def_m,4))
print(round(def_mm,1))

traps: Keeping the real supports instead of transforming them first.
Applying M/EI as a moment. It is a distributed load q*=M/EI.
Swapping the results: conjugate shear gives slope, conjugate moment gives deflection.
Forgetting units: M/EI is 1/m, so V* is radians and M* is metres.

quiz.q: State the two conjugate beam results.
What other name is used for the conjugate beam method?
Why does a real fixed end become a conjugate free end?
quiz.a: Real fixed has zero slope and zero deflection, so conjugate shear and moment must both be zero.

quiz.q: Why does a real simple support stay a simple support?
quiz.a: Real deflection is zero but slope is not, so conjugate moment is zero but shear is not.

quiz.q: For the worked example, what is the total conjugate load and each conjugate reaction?
A simply supported beam span L has central load P and constant EI. Find midspan deflection by the conjugate beam method.
A student keeps the real fixed support in the conjugate beam. What boundary condition is wrong?
quiz.a: The conjugate fixed support can carry nonzero shear and moment, but the real fixed end needs V*=0 and M*=0, so it predicts nonzero slope and deflection there.

beyond: Not for the exam. Structural analysis software usually solves beams by stiffness or finite element methods, not by conjugate beams. The conjugate beam still appears in influence lines and in hand checks of determinate members. It also helps in beam-column problems where the M/EI load includes axial effects. Search for conjugate beam influence lines and virtual work if you want the next step.
